extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literary criticism / general educated readers of 19th-century lectures
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative principles for judging 'the Hero' and the Poet (the Vates) as explained in a 19th-century lecture on poetic greatness, sincerity, and the moral/aesthetic functions of great men. Focuses on what makes a prophet/hero/poet authentic and great.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity (the first and last merit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity is presented as 'the merit of the Koran' and 'the first and last merit in a book' — the fundamental quality that gives rise to all other merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues sincerity 'gives rise to merits of all kinds' and is 'at bottom, it alone can give rise to merit of any kind.' Sincerity appears in directness of utterance, lack of cant, and the presence of genuine conviction; it is exemplified by Mahomet's repeated, earnest appeals and the 'eye that flashes direct into the heart of things.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct insight / sincerity of vision
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet/prophet must have an immediate, first-hand perception of reality — 'the eye that flashes direct into the heart of things' and 'sincerity of vision; the test of a sincere heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterized by rugged directness and rugged vigor of perception (examples: Mahomet noticing clouds, cattle, ships, human compassion). This direct insight is contrasted with borrowed praises or hearsay; the authentic Vates speaks from living contact with the world, not repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief and conviction that leads to living by the creed
rubrics_metrics.description: True greatness involves wholehearted belief and attempt to live by that belief: 'These Arabs believe their religion, and try to live by it!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text values belief not merely as doctrine but as lived practice that shapes a people's life. For a religious or prophetic figure (and analogously for a poet), conviction that is practiced and believed by followers is a mark of authenticity and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness / absence of dilettantism
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest figures are in deadly earnest about their mission; 'No Dilettantism... it is a business of Reprobation and Salvation' — dilettantism is the 'sorest sin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dilettantism or speculative amateurism is condemned as the root of other failures: the great man must not toy with truth. The standard emphasizes a seriousness that makes moral and existential stakes unambiguous (e.g., views of Time and Eternity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical thought / poetic musicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is identified with 'musical Thought' — metrical, musical quality in conception and utterance is the hallmark of the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a delineation is 'authentically musical... in heart and substance' it is poetic. A 'musical thought' penetrates the inmost harmony or melody of a thing; 'All inmost things... naturally utter themselves in Song.' The guide emphasizes rhythm, tune, and inner harmony in language and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penetration of the 'open secret' (divine idea of the world)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vates (Poet/Prophet) must penetrate and reveal the 'sacred mystery of the Universe' — the 'open secret' or divine idea behind appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central vocational criterion: the poet/prohet 'has penetrated into it' and is 'sent hither to make it more impressively known.' Both prophet (moral revelation) and poet (aesthetic revelation) partake in this disclosure; the best work makes that inner reality felt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicating infinitude / Unendlichkeit
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should communicate a sense of infinitude ('Unendlichkeit') — a quality of scope or depth that suggests the limitless or the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture cites German critics who claim the poet has an 'infinitude' in him; this manifests as work that conveys vastness, universal reach, or a feeling of the infinite rather than mere local or trivial concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of moral and aesthetic (Beautiful includes the Good)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's revelation includes both beauty and goodness: the aesthetic and moral insights are intertwined; 'The Beautiful... is higher than the Good; the Beautiful includes in it the Good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Vates may emphasize the aesthetic side while the prophet emphasizes the moral, but they overlap: the highest utterances show what we are to love as well as what we are to do (example: 'Consider the lilies of the field').

rubrics_metrics.name: Lived experience and active engagement (not mere armchair composition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet who has only sat and composed in a chair cannot authentically render heroic life: 'He could not sing the Heroic warrior, unless he himself were at least a Heroic warrior too.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture stresses that poets often must have potential or lived capacities across roles (soldier, statesman, etc.) — lived experience or at least genuine affinity with the sphere depicted is necessary for depth and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great heart and clear, deep-seeing eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential personal qualities: a 'great heart' and 'clear deep-seeing eye' are prerequisites of poetic greatness and of the Hero generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These traits appear repeatedly as the root of all high achievement: courage, vision, sympathy, and intellectual depth. They underlie the ability to be universal and to move others (examples: Napoleon, Burns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality / capacity to embody the general in the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: A universal poet/hero transcends local limits: 'One who rises so far above the general level... will seem a Universal Poet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the distinction between ordinary and universal is partly arbitrary, critics judge greatness by the degree to which a poet's work embodies universal human experience — the ability to make particular stories or images speak to all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion expressed as musical speech (accent and chant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Passionate language naturally becomes musical; accent, chant, and the 'tune' of a people's speech are poetic resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lecture notes that 'all passionate language does of itself become musical' and that even local accents are forms of chant; effective poetic language harnesses that natural music to reach the listener's heart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity over polished respectability (avoidance of insincere cleanliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Insincere polish and respectability are criticized: 'the insincere man... most cleanly, -- just as carbonic acid is, which is death and poison.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard privileges frank, rough, and honest expression over smooth, marketable respectability. The text holds that falsehoods uttered by a sincere man are 'truer' than the truths of an insincere respectable person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to inspire collective belief and social transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: A great prophet/hero/poet can ignite belief in a people and effect historical transformation: 'Belief is great, life-giving... within one century... Arabia is at Grenada on this hand, at Delhi on that.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative attention is given to social impact — whether the teaching or art becomes a living force shaping a nation's life. Power to galvanize followers and create lasting cultural change is a mark of greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral proportionality (justice tempered, measured revenge)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral prescriptions should avoid extremes: Islam is described as allowing measured revenge 'in measure, not overmuch, or beyond justice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text accepts that the moral code may differ from other traditions but praises proportionality and a tendency toward equity (e.g., the institutionalized almsgiving: 'the tenth part... is the property of the poor'). This counts as a moral-aesthetic quality of a movement or leader.
